Thanks again for the time today, Mike — good conversation. Quick recap and next steps so we have alignment before we draft formal SLA language.

Recap of requirements you shared:
- Target latency: p95 targets for request completion (you mentioned ~300ms for most interactive flows).
- Streaming: low time-to-first-token and stable per-token delta for live sessions (customer UX depends on both).
- Concurrency/throughput: baseline of 50 concurrent active sessions with burst to 250; peak token throughput ~5k tokens/s.
- Reporting: monthly SLO reporting and quarterly reviews.

Open clarifying questions from our side (can you confirm in reply):
1) For latency, do you want us to measure time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming and time-to-response-complete for non-streaming, or a single end-to-end tail latency metric?
2) Expected payload size (avg tokens per request) and typical session length for streaming? That helps estimate batching and KV cache benefits.
3) Any procurement/contract constraints (SLA remedy caps, maximum allowable credit)?

Attached: acme-performance-requirements.xlsx (your traffic profile copy) and our initial redwood-draft-sla-2026.pdf with draft language for measurement and remedies.

Proposed next steps:
- Mike: confirm answers to the 3 clarifying Qs above by Thursday.
- We (Marissa + Rachel): update the draft SLA and provide suggested SLO thresholds based on your traffic profile.
- Schedule 30-min follow-up next week with procurement + engineering to finalize language.

Thanks Marissa — appreciate the clear recap. A few answers and clarifications:

1) Latency: We care about two things separately: time-to-first-token for streaming UX (ideally p95 < 150ms) and end-to-end completion latency for non-streaming calls (p95 < 300ms). We'll want both defined in the SLA so we can measure regressions independently.

2) Payload: Average request is ~120 tokens. Streaming sessions typical length 30–90 seconds, average tokens per session ~600. Concurrency: baseline 50, but we need guaranteed behavior up to 200 concurrent streaming sessions for our initial deployment.

3) Remedies: Our procurement team prefers a simple crediting structure (sliding scale of service credits) and a clear monthly reporting cadence. I don't have a hard cap requirement yet — procurement will flag if anything looks off.

Also call out exclusions: scheduled maintenance windows, force majeure, and customer-side network issues. We'll want to see how you define "scheduled maintenance" and what notice looks like.

Let's aim to get the draft SLA updated with explicit measurement definitions and examples of excluded events. We can loop procurement into the next call.

Best,

Thanks Mike — that helps a lot. I've updated the draft SLA to include explicit measurement definitions and an exclusions section. High level language (please review and comment):

- Measurement windows: SLOs are evaluated over a rolling 30-day window unless otherwise noted. Latency metrics reported are the p95 and p99 of observed request latencies.
- Non-streaming latency: measured as time from request acceptance by Redwood's public API to final token delivered to the client (end-to-end at Redwood boundary).
- Streaming latency: two metrics: (1) time-to-first-token measured from request acceptance to first token emitted; (2) per-token inter-arrival delta measured per session.
- Concurrency/throughput: concurrency is defined as the number of concurrently active inference sessions (open streaming websocket or active request). Throughput is measured in tokens/sec aggregated across the tenant.
- Exclusions: scheduled maintenance (>= 72 hours notice if > 4 hours), force majeure, customer network issues, and third-party provider outages beyond Redwood's control.
- Reporting cadence: monthly automated SLO report + dashboard access; quarterly SLA review and tuning.
- Remedies: service credits on a sliding scale for months where SLA targets are missed (example tiers in attached draft). Cap on credits not to exceed 50% of monthly invoice unless otherwise negotiated.

I've attached redwood-draft-sla-2026.pdf with this language and examples. Rachel will follow up with suggested numeric thresholds based on the traffic profile you supplied (thanks for the spreadsheet).

If this reads ok, can we tentatively schedule a Friday 30-min call with your procurement and engineering to finalize?

Marissa

Hi Mike — quick technical notes to make sure the SLA is measurable and implementable on our side.

Measurement specifics we use internally (proposed to include in SLA):
- Measurement point: latencies are measured at Redwood's edge (API gateway) as the time between request acceptance and final byte egress toward the client. For streaming, we report both time-to-first-byte and inter-token deltas measured at the same egress point. This avoids customer-side network skew.
- Rolling window details: rolling 30-day window with daily buckets; SLO is evaluated on the aggregated distribution from those buckets.
- Concurrency definition: an active streaming session is any websocket/HTTP-streaming connection that has not been closed. For sync calls concurrency is active in-flight requests.
- Batching and warm-up: we treat model warm-up and cache-population effects as part of normal operations, but we can exclude an initial 48-hour warm-up after a scheduled model variant rollout if requested.
- Failover/fallback: if we automatically route to a compatible model variant (lower perf) during capacity constraints, that counts as a degraded result — we will report these events separately and they will be excluded from latency SLO calculations if the routing was triggered by an external provider outage (subject to verification).

Suggested numeric thresholds (based on the profile in acme-performance-requirements.xlsx):
- Non-streaming: p95 < 350ms at sustained concurrency of 100, p99 < 800ms.
- Streaming: time-to-first-token p95 < 150ms; per-token inter-arrival p99 < 40ms at sustained throughput 5k tokens/s.
- Throughput/Concurrency guarantees: baseline guaranteed concurrency 50; guaranteed burst to 200 for up to 10 minutes; sustained throughput SLA target 5k tokens/s with 95% availability.

Related links: sample performance dashboard (https://drive.redwood.com/shared/acme/perf-dashboard-sample) and a support ticket template we use for SLA breaches (https://support.redwood.com/tickets/templates/sla-breach).

We can include these definitions verbatim in the SLA draft so procurement has a clear, testable spec. If Acme expects a different measurement point (for example client-side metrics), we'll need a joint runbook for joint measurement and reconciliation.

Would you be able to share typical time-of-day traffic patterns? That will affect batching behavior and our suggested thresholds.

Thanks,
Rachel Kim
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
